passage:
Dear Salma,

I've been meaning to write since our chat last week. You asked how training is going, and I said "fine". It isn't. I'm training to become a translator, and every week there's a new video of an AI translating a page in seconds. Last night I lay awake doing the maths on whether I'll have a job in five years. My chest gets tight just typing that.

I know the worry makes sense. But I also know freezing won't help. So I've started using the tools for first drafts and correcting them, which is teaching me where they get tone and idiom wrong. That feels like a skill.

Can we talk this weekend about which human parts of the work I should get better at?

Kiran

qa.q: What is Kiran training to become?
qa.a: Kiran is training to become a translator.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about the future, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kiran is anxious: lying awake doing the maths on a job in five years and feeling the chest get tight.

qa.q: What is Kiran doing that is wiser than freezing or denial?
qa.a: Kiran uses the tools for first drafts and corrects them, learning where they miss tone and idiom, and wants to build the human parts of the work.

qa.q: How might Salma react to Kiran's letter?
qa.a: Salma may be touched that Kiran finally admitted it isn't fine, and the question about human skills invites a practical talk instead of reassurance alone.

grounding: Kiran worries AI will take the job Kiran is training for and responds by learning the tools and building judgement rather than freezing.

passage:
Dear Minakshi ma'am,

You told us at the workshop that we could write to you, so I am. I'm in my final year of the translation diploma, and last week my cousin showed me a free tool that turned a whole Marathi short story into English in ten seconds. It was not perfect, but it was not bad either.

Since then I can't sleep properly. I keep thinking I have spent three years training for a job that will vanish before I start. Some days I want to switch courses; some days I tell myself it's all hype and ignore it.

I know neither of those is really a plan. Could you tell me which skills you think a machine can't do well, and whether it is worth learning to edit machine translations? I would rather learn than freeze.

With respect,
Deepika

qa.q: How long did the free tool take to translate the Marathi short story?
What is Deepika feeling since seeing the tool, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Deepika feels anxious and unsettled about the future, losing sleep and swinging between switching courses and ignoring it.

qa.q: What wise step is Deepika already taking?
qa.a: Deepika is asking a mentor which human skills matter and whether to learn to edit machine translations, choosing to adapt instead of freezing or denying.

qa.q: How might Minakshi ma'am see Deepika's letter?
qa.a: Minakshi ma'am may feel touched to be trusted, and see a student whose fear is understandable and who wants practical guidance.

grounding: The letter shows a student anxious that AI will take the job Deepika is training for, choosing to learn and adapt rather than freeze or deny.

passage:
Raghav, you asked what scares me, so here's the real answer. I'm Aparna, final year in graphic design. Last semester, a client I'd done posters for sent me a note: "Thanks, we'll use the AI generator from now on." That was it. Three years of drawing and I lost a job to a text box.

For a month I didn't open my sketchbook. I told everyone AI art was a fad. Honestly, I was terrified.

What changed was a small thing. My professor asked us to use the generator for twenty ideas, then pick one and make it real, for an actual shop owner with actual problems. The machine gave pretty pictures. The shop owner needed someone to listen about why nobody noticed her sign. That part was me.

I'm learning the tools now. I'm also learning to ask better questions.

qa.q: What did the client's note say?
qa.a: The note said, "Thanks, we'll use the AI generator from now on."

qa.q: How did Aparna feel after losing the client, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aparna felt terrified, which shows in not opening the sketchbook for a month and insisting AI art was a fad.

qa.q: What helped Aparna move from fear to action?
qa.a: The professor's exercise showed that the machine gives ideas but a real client needs someone who listens, so Aparna started learning the tools and building those human skills.

qa.q: How might the shop owner see Aparna's role compared with the generator?
qa.a: The shop owner likely values Aparna for listening and solving the real problem, which a picture generator alone could not do.

grounding: The monologue shows a design student afraid AI will take the work, who moves from denial to learning the tools and building human skills.
